payload.name: superior-pharyngeal-constrictor
payload.scope: People made the superior-pharyngeal-constrictor construct to map the uppermost pharyngeal constrictor muscle band that forms the posterior and lateral walls of the superior pharynx, enabling clinicians to localize pharyngeal constriction defects and retropharyngeal abscesses.

definition.body: The superior pharyngeal constrictor is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the quadrate sheet of muscle forming the uppermost band of the posterior and lateral walls of the pharynx. Parameters: (1) the origins - pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe (shared with the buccinator), and the medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone; (2) the insertion - the pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone and the pharyngeal raphe, a midline tendon where the fibers of both sides interdigitate; (3) the fiber orientation - lower fibers run inferiorly, upper fibers overlap the middle constrictor; (4) the aperture - the stylopharyngeus nerve passes through between the superior and middle bands; (5) the clinical significance - landmark for pharyngeal surgery, origin of superior constrictor palsy in stroke, and site of pharyngoplasty for velopharyngeal insufficiency. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology references, and swallowing assessment protocols. e.g.: the superior pharyngeal constrictor in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the pharyngeal raphe during constrictor repair in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; stylopharyngeus nerve passing through the constrictor in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition | not: the middle-pharyngeal-constrictor (the intermediate band arising from the hyoid bone, a distinct muscle layer); the inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor arising from the cricoid and thyroid cartilages, a distinct muscle layer; the buccinator (the facial muscle sharing the pterygomandibular raphe, not a pharyngeal muscle) [formal: constrictor pharyngis superior | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: People made the middle-pharyngeal-constrictor construct to map the intermediate pharyngeal constrictor muscle band arising from the hyoid apparatus, enabling clinicians to assess swallowing mechanics and pharyngeal wall abnormalities.

definition.body: The middle pharyngeal constrictor is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the fan-shaped sheet of muscle forming the intermediate band of the posterior and lateral walls of the pharynx. Parameters: (1) the origins - the lesser and greater horns of the hyoid bone and the hyoidothyroid ligament; (2) the insertion - the pharyngeal raphe and overlapping fibers posteriorly where it fuses with the superior constrictor above and the inferior constrictor below; (3) the fiber arrangement - fibers fan superiorly to overlap the superior constrictor and inferiorly to be overlapped by the inferior constrictor; (4) the aperture - the stylopharyngeus muscle passes between the superior and middle constrictors, and the glossopharyngeal nerve and tonsillar artery pass between the middle and inferior constrictors; (5) the clinical significance - landmark in tonsillectomy (the constrictor is the bed from which the tonsil is dissected), site of pharyngeal diverticula, and reference for pharyngeal pacing. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology references, and swallowing assessment protocols. e.g.: the middle pharyngeal constrictor in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the tonsil bed defined by the middle constrictor in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; stylopharyngeus passing between the constrictors in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition | not: superior-pharyngeal-constrictor (uppermost band from pterygoid, distinct layer); inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor (lowest band from cricoid/thyroid, distinct layer); stylopharyngeus (passes between constrictors, not a constrictor) [formal: constrictor pharyngis medius | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The inferior pharyngeal constrictor is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the lowest and broadest band of muscle forming the posterior and lateral walls of the inferior pharynx. Parameters: (1) the origins - the oblique and transverse parts arising from the cricoid cartilage (thyrocricoid membrane and posterior lamina) and the thyroid cartilage (oblique line); (2) the insertion - the pharyngeal raphe posteriorly where fibers from both sides interdigitate; (3) the fiber arrangement - lower fibers run horizontally to the raphe, upper fibers (cricopharyngeus part) run obliquely upward and medially, forming the lower boundary of the inferior constrictor; (4) the apertures - the esophagus passes through inferiorly at the pharyngoesophageal junction, the internal laryngeal nerve pierces between the superior and inferior bands, and the superior laryngeal artery passes through the same gap; (5) the clinical significance - the cricopharyngeus part forms the upper esophageal sphincter (Cricopharyngeal dysfunction causes dysphagia and Zenker's diverticulum through Killian's dehiscence between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology references, and swallowing assessment protocols. e.g.: the inferior pharyngeal constrictor in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the cricopharyngeal bar seen on barium swallow per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; Killian's dehiscence at the thyropharyngeus-cricopharyngeus junction in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition | not: middle-pharyngeal-constrictor (intermediate band from hyoid, distinct layer); superior-pharyngeal-constrictor (uppermost band from pterygoid, distinct layer); cricopharyngeus-muscle (the transverse band forming the upper esophageal sphincter, a specialized part of this muscle) [formal: constrictor pharyngis inferior | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: postcricoid-region
payload.scope: People made the postcricoid region construct to map the hypopharyngeal subsite behind the cricoid cartilage so that clinicians can localize cancers, assess swallowing pathology, and plan esophageal surgery.

definition.body: The postcricoid region is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the subsite of the hypopharynx located posterior to the cricoid cartilage and anterior to the esophagus, whose boundaries are used in swallowing assessment and oncological staging. Parameters: (1) the anatomical boundaries — anteriorly defined by the posterior surface of the cricoid cartilage, laterally continuous with the pyriform sinuses, posteriorly by the esophageal mucosa, and superiorly by the aryepiglottic folds; (2) the mucosal characteristics — stratified squamous epithelium forming the postcricoid mucosa, continuous with adjacent hypopharyngeal and esophageal mucosa; (3) the clinical significance — common site for hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, region evaluated for postcricoid webs and rings, landmark for esophageal opening during endoscopy. It persists as a maintained anatomical subsite in head-and-neck anatomy, TNM oncology staging systems, and otolaryngology. e.g.: the postcricoid region defined as a hypopharyngeal subsite in AJCC 8th edition TNM staging for hypopharyngeal carcinoma; postcricoid web identified as a cause of dysphagia on barium swallow study; postcricoid squamous cell carcinoma assessed during upper endoscopy for surgical resection planning | not: the cricoid-cartilage (the supporting bony structure, not the mucosal region); the pyriform-sinus (the lateral recess, a separate subsite of the hypopharynx); the esophagus (the tube beginning at the cricoid level, distinct from the hypopharyngeal region) [formal: regio postcricodea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pharyngeal-recess
payload.scope: People made the pharyngeal recess construct to map the depression in the superior-posterior nasopharynx so that clinicians can identify the most common site of nasopharyngeal carcinoma origin, assess nasopharyngeal disease, and plan oncological treatment.

definition.body: The pharyngeal recess is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the narrow depression in the superior-posterior wall of the nasopharynx, also known as Fossa of Rosenmüller, whose boundaries are critical landmarks in nasopharyngeal carcinoma staging. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly by the superior pharyngeal constrictor, superiorly by the basilar part of the occipital bone, posteriorly by the upper fibers of the superior constrictor; (2) the contents — the pharyngeal tonsil tissue may extend into the recess; (3) the clinical significance — most common site of origin for nasopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, region assessed by nasopharyngoscopy. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in otolaryngology, head-and-neck oncology, and nasopharyngeal disease evaluation. e.g.: the pharyngeal recess (Fossa of Rosenmüller) described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; the pharyngeal recess as the common origin site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma in AJCC 8th edition staging; nasopharyngoscopy visualization of the pharyngeal recess during epistaxis evaluation | not: the nasopharynx (the complete region containing this recess); the pharyngeal-tonsil (the lymphoid tissue that may extend into the recess); the auditory-tube (the structure opening nearby, not the recess itself) [formal: recessus pharyngeus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: stylopharyngeus-muscle
payload.scope: People made the stylopharyngeus muscle construct to map the unique longitudinal pharyngeal muscle that elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing so that clinicians can assess cranial nerve IX function, plan pharyngeal surgery, and evaluate swallowing disorders.

definition.body: The stylopharyngeus muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired longitudinal muscle of the pharynx originating from the styloid process, whose unique course passes between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors to elevate the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and speech. Parameters: (1) the origin — apex of the styloid process and its associated stylohyoid ligament; (2) the course — descends along the lateral pharyngeal wall, passing between the superior and middle constrictor muscles to insert into the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage; (3) the innervation — glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), the only pharyngeal muscle with this innervation; (4) the action — elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and speech, widens the pharyngeal cavity; (5) the clinical significance — landmark in tonsillectomy surgery, its atrophy assessed in glossopharyngeal nerve palsy, and its course relevant to transstyloid surgical approaches to the parapharyngeal space. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in head-and-neck anatomy, otolaryngology, and cranial nerve assessment. e.g.: stylopharyngeus described in Gray's Anatomy as sole muscle between constrictors; stylopharyngeus course between constrictors visualized during tonsillectomy; glossopharyngeal nerve palsy assessed via stylopharyngeus-mediated pharyngeal elevation | not: the stylohyoid-muscle (the digastric-related muscle also from the styloid process, innervated by CN VII); the superior-pharyngeal-constrictor (a constrictor muscle, not a longitudinal elevator); the glossopharyngeal-nerve (the nerve that innervates this muscle, not the muscle itself) [formal: musculus stylopharyngeus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: salpingopharyngeus-muscle
payload.scope: People made the salpingopharyngeus muscle construct to map the longitudinal pharyngeal muscle that elevates the pharynx from the auditory tube origin so that clinicians can assess swallowing function, evaluate nasopharyngeal disease, and plan head-and-neck surgery.

definition.body: The salpingopharyngeus muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired longitudinal muscle of the pharynx originating from the cartilaginous part of the auditory tube, whose fibers merge with the palatopharyngeus to form the salpingopharyngeal fold and elevate the pharynx during swallowing. Parameters: (1) the origin — the cartilaginous portion of the auditory (Eustachian) tube near the torus tubarius; (2) the course — descends along the lateral pharyngeal wall as a narrow muscular band, blending inferiorly with the palatopharyngeus muscle; (3) the insertion — posterior border of the thyroid cartilage and the pharyngeal wall; (4) the action — elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and speech; (5) the clinical significance — forms the salpingopharyngeal fold visible on nasopharyngoscopy, landmark for identifying the auditory tube opening in nasopharyngeal carcinoma staging, relevant in pediatric adenoidectomy. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in otolaryngology, cranial nerve assessment, and nasopharyngeal disease evaluation. e.g.: salpingopharyngeus muscle in Gray's Anatomy as part of the palatopharyngeal complex; salpingopharyngeal fold visualized during nasopharyngoscopy; salpingopharyngeus function in pharyngeal elevation during swallowing assessed by videofluoroscopy | not: the palatopharyngeus-muscle (the adjacent muscle blending with it, a distinct muscle); the auditory-tube (the cartilaginous structure providing origin, not the muscle itself); the levator-veli-palatini (another muscle associated with the auditory tube, innervated differently) [formal: musculus salpingopharyngeus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: palatopharyngeus-muscle
payload.scope: People made the palatopharyngeus muscle construct to map the longitudinal pharyngeal muscle that elevates the pharynx from the soft palate origin so that clinicians can assess swallowing function, evaluate velopharyngeal disorders, and plan palatal surgery.

definition.body: The palatopharyngeus muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired longitudinal muscle of the pharynx originating from the soft palate, whose fibers descend to merge with the salpingopharyngeus and insert into the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage, elevating the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and forming the posterior tonsillar pillar. Parameters: (1) the origin — the palatopharyngeal aponeurosis from the posterior border of the soft palate (palatine aponeurosis); (2) the course — descends along the lateral pharyngeal wall as a muscular band; (3) the fusion — merges with the salpingopharyngeus muscle superiorly; (4) the insertion — posterior border of the thyroid cartilage and the pharyngeal wall; (5) the clinical significance — forms the palatopharyngeal fold (posterior tonsillar pillar) visible on oropharyngeal inspection, its function impaired in velopharyngeal insufficiency. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in head-and-neck anatomy, otolaryngology, and swallowing assessment. e.g.: palatopharyngeus described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition as part of the palatopharyngeal complex; palatopharyngeal fold visualized on oral examination as the posterior tonsillar pillar; palatopharyngeus weakness assessed in velopharyngeal dysfunction per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition | not: the salpingopharyngeus-muscle (the superior muscle that blends with it, originating from the auditory tube); the levator-veli-palatini (a separate soft palate muscle originating from the temporal bone, innervated differently); the tensor-veli-palatini (another soft palate muscle not part of the longitudinal pharyngeal muscle group) [formal: musculus palatopharyngeus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: palatine-tonsil
payload.scope: People made the palatine-tonsil construct to map the paired lymphoid tissue masses embedded in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, so that clinicians can diagnose tonsillitis, distinguish normal lymphoid tissue from neoplasia, and plan tonsillectomy.

definition.body: The palatine tonsil is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired oval masses of lymphoid tissue located in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches at the junction of the oral cavity and oropharynx. Parameters: (1) the location — bilateral tonsillar fossae bounded anteriorly by the palatoglossal arch (palatoglossus muscle) and posteriorly by the palatopharyngeal arch (palatopharyngeus muscle) in the lateral oropharyngeal wall; (2) the lymphoid architecture — a central core of lymphoid follicles with germinal centers, covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium that invaginates to form 10–20 crypts; (3) the blood supply — tonsillar branch of the facial artery as the principal supply, with contributions from the ascending palatine artery, dorsal lingual arteries, and descending palatine artery; (4) the innervation — glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via tonsillar branches for sensory innervation and the tonsillar plexus, plus the lesser palatine nerves; (5) the clinical significance — common site of bacterial colonization (Group A Streptococcus), recurrent tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess formation, and tonsillar hypertrophy causing obstructive sleep apnea. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in otolaryngology, head and neck surgery, and clinical examination. e.g.: the palatine tonsil as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; tonsillectomy specimen showing lymphoid follicles and crypt architecture on histology per Bailey's Head and Neck Surgery; tonsillar hypertrophy grading on lateral neck radiograph used in pediatric sleep apnea assessment | not: the lingual-tonsil (the lymphoid tissue at the base of the tongue, a distinct mass); the nasopharyngeal-tonsil (adenoid, lymphoid tissue in the nasopharynx, a separate structure); the tubal-tonsil (Gerlach's tonsil, lymphoid tissue near the Eustachian tube opening) [formal: tonsilla palatina | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lingual-tonsil
payload.scope: People made the lingual-tonsil construct to map the collection of lymphoid tissue at the posterior third of the tongue base, so that clinicians can assess lingual tonsillar hypertrophy causing obstructive sleep apnea, plan lingual tonsillectomy, and distinguish lingual tonsil tissue from base-of-tongue neoplasia.

definition.body: The lingual tonsil is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the diffuse collection of lymphoid tissue located on the posterior one-third (dorsal surface) of the tongue base, extending from the circumvallate papillae anteriorly to the epiglottic folds posteriorly and bounded laterally by the vallecula. Parameters: (1) the location — dorsal surface of the posterior tongue base within the oral portion of the oropharynx, between the circumvallate papillae and the epiglottis; (2) the histological architecture — multiple small lymphoid nodules without the deep crypt system of the palatine tonsil, covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the tongue mucosa; (3) the lymphoid distribution — nodules arranged on both sides of the midline with variable midline continuity, each containing germinal centers; (4) the innervation — glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) for sensory innervation of the posterior tongue base and lingual nerve (CN V3) for anterior lingual tonsillar region; (5) the clinical significance — potential site of lingual tonsillar hypertrophy causing obstructive sleep apnea, lingual tonsillectomy as a surgical procedure, and lymphoid malignancy. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in otolaryngology, sleep medicine, and head and neck surgery. e.g.: the lingual tonsil as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; lingual tonsil hypertrophy graded on flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy per LSO classification; lingual tonsillectomy specimen showing lymphoid tissue on histology | not: the palatine-tonsil (the paired oval masses in the oropharyngeal lateral walls, a distinct anatomical structure); the nasopharyngeal-tonsil (adenoid, lymphoid tissue in the nasopharynx, a separate structure) [formal: tonsilla lingualis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: bronchiole
payload.scope: People made the bronchiole construct to map the terminal airway branches within the lung parenchyma distal to the bronchi, so that clinicians can diagnose bronchiolar disease, understand airflow regulation, and interpret pulmonary pathology.

definition.body: The bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the terminal branches of the conducting airways within the lung parenchyma, distal to the terminal bronchioles, that continue air conduction toward the alveolar gas-exchange units. Parameters: (1) the caliber — diameters ranging from approximately 1 mm in the larger bronchioles to less than 0.5 mm, decreasing distally through successive generations (Weibel model generation 14-23); (2) the wall architecture — walls composed of smooth muscle and elastic fibers without cartilage plates or submucosal glands, lined by simple cuboidal epithelium in terminal bronchioles transitioning to simple squamous in respiratory bronchioles; (3) the mucociliary apparatus — ciliated cells and Clara (club) cells secreting surfactant proteins and protease inhibitors, with diminishing ciliated surface area distally; (4) the bronchial smooth muscle — circularly arranged smooth muscle forming a thicker proportion of the wall relative to diameter, regulating airflow through bronchoconstriction and bronchodilation; (5) the respiratory division — respiratory bronchioles as transitional structures with scattered alveoli budding from their walls, marking the onset of gas exchange within the conduction pathway. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in pulmonology, histology, and respiratory pathophysiology. e.g.: the bronchiole histology as described in Junqueira's Basic Histology; bronchiolar smooth muscle constriction measured during bronchoprovocation testing per ATS guidelines; club cell secretory protein (CC16) quantified in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid | not: the terminal-bronchiole (smallest conducting bronchiole, transitional subregion); the alveolus (the gas-exchange unit distal to the bronchial tree, a distinct structure) [formal: bronchiolus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: alveolus
payload.scope: People made the alveolus construct to map the microscopic air sac within the lung where gas exchange between air and blood occurs, so that clinicians can diagnose pulmonary gas exchange disorders, understand ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and interpret interstitial lung disease.

definition.body: The alveolus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the microscopic thin-walled air sac within the lung parenchyma where oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse between the air and the pulmonary capillary blood. Parameters: (1) the wall architecture — a single layer of type I alveolar cells (pneumocytes) covering approximately 97% of the alveolar surface area, optimized for gas diffusion; (2) the surfactant-producing cells — type II alveolar cells (pneumocytes) comprising the remaining 3% of surface area, secreting pulmonary surfactant composed of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine and surfactant proteins A through D to reduce surface tension; (3) the alveolar-capillary membrane — the combined barrier of type I cell cytoplasm, fused basal laminae, and capillary endothelium, approximately 0.2-0.5 micrometers thick at its thinnest point; (4) the alveolar macrophages — resident immune cells (dust cells) on the alveolar surface phagocytosing inhaled particles and pathogens; (5) the alveolar duct and sac architecture — alveoli arranged in clusters along alveolar ducts and at the walls of alveolar sacs, forming the functional gas-exchange units of the lung acinus. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in pulmonology, histology, and respiratory physiology. e.g.: the alveolus as described in West's Respiratory Physiology, 10th edition; lung biopsy specimen showing type I and type II pneumocytes on electron microscopy; surfactant replacement therapy for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome per American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines | not: the bronchiole (the conducting airway proximal to the alveolus, a distinct structure); the respiratory-bronchiole (the transitional airway with scattered alveoli, a different structure) [formal: alveolus pulmonis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pleura
payload.scope: People made the pleura construct to map the double-layered serous membrane enclosing the lungs and lining the thoracic cavity, so that clinicians can diagnose pleural disease, interpret chest imaging, and manage pleural effusions.

definition.body: The pleura is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the double-layered serous membrane that envelops the lungs and lines the thoracic cavity, creating a closed potential space whose thin fluid layer enables frictionless respiratory movement. Parameters: (1) the two layers — the visceral pleura adhering directly to the lung surface including the interlobar fissures, and the parietal pleura lining the thoracic wall, divided into costal (rib-facing), diaphragmatic (diaphragm-facing), mediastinal (midline), and cervical (cupula) regions; (2) the pleural cavity — the potential space between the visceral and parietal layers containing approximately 10-20 mL of serous fluid, maintaining negative intrapleural pressure essential for lung expansion; (3) the pleural reflection lines — anatomical lines where the parietal pleura transitions between regions, forming recesses (costodiaphragmatic and costomediastinal) that allow lung expansion during deep inspiration; (4) the blood supply — visceral pleura supplied by bronchial arteries, parietal pleura supplied by intercostal and internal thoracic arteries, with venous drainage following arterial patterns; (5) the innervation — parietal pleura innervated by somatic nerves (intercostal nerves for costal and diaphragmatic pleura, phrenic nerve for mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura), visceral pleura innervated by autonomic fibers with no pain sensation. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in radiology, thoracic surgery, and pulmonary medicine. e.g.: the pleura as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; pleural effusion visualized as blunting of the costodiaphragmatic recess on upright chest radiograph; thoracentesis procedure performed under ultrasound guidance per American College of Chest Physicians guidelines | not: the pleural-cavity (the potential space between the two layers of pleura, a distinct structure); the costal-pleura (the parietal pleura lining the ribs, a regional substructure) [formal: pleura | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

Parameters: (1) the two layers — the visceral pleura adhering directly to the lung surface including the interlobar fissures, and the parietal pleura lining the thoracic wall, divided into costal (rib-facing), diaphragmatic (diaphragm-facing), mediastinal (midline), and cervical (cupula) regions; (2) the pleural cavity — the potential space between the visceral and parietal layers containing approximately 10-20 mL of serous fluid, maintaining negative intrapleural pressure essential for lung expansion; (3) the pleural reflection lines — anatomical lines where the parietal pleura transitions between regions, forming recesses (costodiaphragmatic and costomediastinal) that allow lung expansion during deep inspiration; (4) the blood supply — visceral pleura supplied by bronchial arteries, parietal pleura supplied by intercostal and internal thoracic arteries, with venous drainage following arterial patterns; (5) the innervation — parietal pleura innervated by somatic nerves (intercostal nerves for costal and diaphragmatic pleura, phrenic nerve for mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura), visceral pleura innervated by autonomic fibers with no pain sensation. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in radiology, thoracic surgery, and pulmonary medicine. e.g.: the pleura as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; pleural effusion visualized as blunting of the costodiaphragmatic recess on upright chest radiograph; thoracentesis procedure performed under ultrasound guidance per American College of Chest Physicians guidelines | not: the pleural-cavity (the potential space between the two layers of pleura, a distinct structure); the costal-pleura (the parietal pleura lining the ribs, a regional substructure) [formal: pleura | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lung
payload.scope: People made the lung construct to map the paired respiratory organs of gas exchange within the thoracic cavity, so that clinicians can diagnose pulmonary disease, interpret chest imaging, and manage respiratory failure.

definition.body: The lung is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired spongy respiratory organs within the thoracic cavity, separated by the mediastinum, in which air is conducted through branching bronchi to alveolar gas-exchange surfaces. Parameters: (1) the lateralization — the right lung (three lobes: upper, middle, and lower, separated by the oblique and horizontal fissures) and the left lung (two lobes: upper and lower, separated by the oblique fissure, with the lingula corresponding to the right middle lobe); (2) the bronchial tree — the hierarchical branching from the main bronchi through lobar, segmental, and subsegmental bronchi to bronchioles and respiratory bronchioles, with cartilage decreasing and smooth muscle increasing toward the periphery; (3) the parenchymal architecture — the functional lung parenchyma composed of alveolar tissue supported by a connective tissue stroma, organized into lobules supplied by terminal bronchioles; (4) the vascular supply — dual blood supply via bronchial arteries (systemic, nutrient supply from the aorta) and pulmonary arteries (gas exchange, deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle), with pulmonary veins draining oxygenated blood to the left atrium; (5) the pleural covering — each lung is enveloped by visceral pleura that extends into the fissures, continuous at the hilum with parietal pleura lining the thoracic cavity. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in pulmonology, thoracic surgery, radiology, and respiratory medicine. e.g.: the lung as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; chest CT showing right lower lobe consolidation in community-acquired pneumonia; wedge resection specimen of pulmonary nodule examined on histology per WHO classification of lung tumors | not: the pleura (the serous membrane enclosing the lung, a distinct structure); the bronchus (the major airway conducting air into the lung, a proximal structure) [formal: pulmon | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: intermediate-tracheal-ligament
payload.scope: People made the intermediate-tracheal ligament construct to map the anterior fibrous band connecting the cricoid cartilage to the first tracheal ring, so that surgeons can identify this landmark during tracheostomy and laryngotracheal surgery.

definition.body: The intermediate-tracheal ligament is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the fibrous band running anteriorly between the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage and the superior border of the first tracheal ring, distinct from the posterior cricotracheal membrane. Parameters: (1) the location — anterior surface of the tracheoesophageal junction, bridging the cricoid lamina inferiorly to the first tracheal ring superiorly; (2) the composition — a condensed band of dense fibrous connective tissue, continuous with the pretracheal fascia; (3) the relationship — lies anterior to the cricotracheal membrane and the inferior thyroid veins; (4) the clinical significance — a landmark for surgical access during tracheostomy and laryngotracheal procedures. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, surgical anatomy references, and airway management atlases. e.g.: the intermediate tracheal ligament described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; the anterior tracheal band identified during surgical tracheostomy in Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th edition; intermediate ligament landmark in the tracheoesophageal junction diagram in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition | not: the cricotracheal membrane (the posterior fibrous band connecting the same two structures); the cricothyroid membrane (the sheet between thyroid and cricoid cartilages, a different region) [formal: ligamentum tracheale intermedium | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

[3 test] The note states the removal test but its stated result does not follow. The SLN's external branch supplies exactly one of the larynx's five carved intrinsic muscles (parameter 3): the cricothyroid. The other four — thyroarytenoid, posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid, interarytenoid — and the sensory supply of the mucosa below the vocal folds ride the RLN, which the larynx's own accepted DEPENDS_ON edge already records. Remove the SLN now: the cricothyroid paralyzes, pitch range narrows, supraglottic sensation is lost — but the larynx's defined operation (air passage plus voice production by the vocal folds and their intrinsic musculature) does not STOP. The folds remain mobile, phonation continues, and airway protection (fold closure, laryngeal reflexes below the folds) is intact via the RLN. The note's 'so the larynx's defined operation of pitch modulation and airway protection stops' overstates the result: degradation is not stoppage, and airway protection plainly does not stop. The accepted larynx-RLN and larynx-vagus edges rest on total loss of the carved musculature; the SLN supplies one of five muscles. As argued, the note fails item 3.

payload.name: mucociliary-escalator
payload.scope: People made the mucociliary escalator construct to map the coordinated mucus-and-cilia mechanism that clears the airway, so that pulmonologists can quantify its dysfunction in diseases like primary ciliary dyskinesia and chronic bronchitis.

definition.body: The mucociliary escalator is a human-authored anatomophysiological construct that maps the coordinated mechanism by which ciliated epithelial cells and mucus-secreting goblet cells in the airway clear particulate matter and pathogens upward. Parameters: (1) the mucous layer — a bilayer: an aqueous periciliary layer (approximately 7 μm) overlaid by a viscous mucus gel (approximately 10 μm) produced by goblet cells and submucosal glands; (2) the ciliary apparatus — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with motile cilia beating at approximately 12-18 Hz, their tips penetrating the periciliary layer to engage the mucus gel; (3) the directionality — unidirectional metachronal waves propelling mucus from the bronchi and trachea toward the oropharynx at rates of approximately 1-2 cm/min; (4) the clearance function — entrapment of inhaled particles, bacteria, and debris in mucus followed by expectoration or swallowing. It persists as a maintained functional concept in pulmonology, respiratory physiology, and airway disease research. e.g.: the mucociliary clearance assay described in the ATS/ERS consensus statement on bronchiectasis (2017); primary ciliary dyskinesia as a disease of failed mucociliary transport per Cotton Pediatric Otolaryngology, 7th edition; mucociliary transport measured by radiolabeled particle clearance in Annals of Otology | not: the mucociliary clearance test (the clinical measurement procedure, not the mechanism itself); the mucociliary system (the broader organ-level concept including all glands and epithelium) [formal: scutum mucociliare | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cough-reflex
payload.scope: People made the cough reflex construct to map the coordinated neurophysiological sequence that clears the airway of irritants, so that pulmonologists and neurologists can diagnose and treat pathological cough syndromes.

definition.body: The cough reflex is a human-authored neurophysiological construct that maps the coordinated three-phase motor sequence — inspiratory effort, glottic closure with intrathoracic pressure buildup, and sudden explosive expiratory glottic opening — triggered by sensory receptors in the upper and lower airways. Parameters: (1) the afferent limb — vagal sensory receptors (cough receptors) in the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and pharynx, stimulated by mechanical irritation, chemical mediators, or inflammatory signals, with the carina being the most sensitive region; (2) the central pattern generator — the cough center in the medulla oblongata that coordinates the sequential activation of inspiratory diaphragm/intercostal muscles, expiratory abdominal/thoracic muscles, and glottic muscles; (3) the expiratory phase — rapid expulsion of air at velocities up to 1000 L/min through the upper airway, generating shear forces that dislodge secretions and foreign bodies; (4) the clinical dysregulation — persistent cough as a symptom of respiratory disease, intractable cough refractory to standard therapy, and the protective vs. pathological distinction. It persists as a maintained functional concept in pulmonology, neurology, and otorhinolaryngology. e.g.: the cough reflex arc described in the ATS position statement on cough (2022); cough receptor sensitivity mapping via capsaicin inhalation challenge per Chung and Griffiths (1999) in Clinical Science; intractable cough management with neuromodulator therapy documented in CHEST, 149(4):1076-1091 | not: the cough center in the medulla (the neural substrate, not the complete reflex construct); cough medicine (the pharmaceutical treatment, not the physiological mechanism) [formal: reflexus tussivus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: People made the endotracheal tube to keep the airway patent during general anesthesia and mechanical ventilation, so that a patient whose airway is unprotected or obstructed can be ventilated and protected from aspiration.

definition.body: The endotracheal tube is a human-made airway device: a single-lumen tube, cuffed or cuffless, with an ISO 535-1 connector, inserted through the mouth or nose past the vocal folds into the trachea and secured there to hold a patent airway. Parameters: (1) the lumen and sizing — internal diameter measured in millimeters, 6.0 to 8.0 mm for adults, with length measured from the tip to the connector; (2) the cuff — a high-volume low-pressure cuff inflated through a pilot balloon to seal against the tracheal wall against ventilation leak and aspiration; (3) the connector — a 15 mm ISO 535-1 female connector for anesthesia circuits and ventilators; (4) the fixation — external security at the lips or teeth by tape or a tube holder, with the depth marked at the incisors; (5) the materials — silicone or polyvinyl chloride, chosen for biocompatibility and resistance to kinking. It persists as standard equipment in every anesthesia and critical-care setting, specified by ISO 535-1 and used in airway-management protocols worldwide. e.g.: ISO 535-1:1989, the international standard specifying endotracheal tube dimensions and test methods; a cuffed 7.0 mm silicone tube placed during rapid-sequence induction per the ASA Difficult Airway Algorithm; neonatal tube sizing by the age/4+4 formula in pediatric anesthesia references | not: the tracheostomy tube (inserted through a surgically created opening in the neck, not through the mouth and vocal folds); the laryngeal mask airway (a supraglottic seal above the laryngeal inlet, not a tube inside the trachea) [formal: tuba trachealis | substrate: matter | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: tracheostomy-tube
payload.scope: People made the tracheostomy tube to maintain a surgical airway below the larynx for patients whose upper airway cannot be kept open, so that long-term ventilation and suctioning are possible.

definition.body: The tracheostomy tube is a human-made airway device inserted through a surgically created stoma in the anterior neck directly into the trachea, bypassing the nose, mouth and larynx. Parameters: (1) the construction — an outer cannula with an inner cannula that can be removed and cleaned in situ, in cuffed and cuffless forms; (2) the sizing — internal diameter from 4 mm in neonates to 8 mm in adults, measured by French or millimeter systems; (3) the fixation — a D-ring or tube holder secured by ties through the neck, with the stoma kept open by the outer cannula; (4) the tracheal opening — a stoma created by surgical tracheostomy or a percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy, the tube passing through it into the tracheal lumen; (5) the clinical use — long-term ventilation, secretion clearance and reduction of dead space in intensive care. It persists as standard equipment in critical-care and respiratory practice, specified by ISO 14810 and used in tracheostomy care protocols worldwide. e.g.: ISO 14810:2009, the international standard for tracheostomy tubes; a 6 mm cuffed tracheostomy tube placed percutaneously at bedside in an ICU patient per the MAST technique; the inner cannula of a standard tracheostomy tube removed for daily cleaning in a tracheostomy care bundle | not: the endotracheal tube (inserted through the mouth or nose past the vocal folds, not through a neck stoma); the laryngostomy tube (implanted in a laryngectomy patient with no larynx, not in an airway that retains the larynx) [formal: tuba tracheotomiae | substrate: matter | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: nasal-cavity
payload.scope: People made the nasal-cavity construct to map the paired air-filled space within the skull that warms, humidifies and filters the inspired air, so that otolaryngologists can localize the conchae, the meatuses and the sinus openings during rhinoscopy and endoscopic sinus surgery.

definition.body: The nasal cavity is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired air-filled space within the skull, bounded above by the nasal bones and the frontal, ethmoid and sphenoid bones, laterally by the maxilla, the ethmoid, the lacrimal, the palatine and the inferior nasal concha, medially by the nasal septum, and open inferiorly into the nasopharynx. Parameters: (1) the vestibule — the anterior portion, lined with skin bearing hair follicles; (2) the conchae and meatuses — the superior, middle and inferior turbinates project into the cavity and form the superior, middle and inferior meatuses; (3) the olfactory region — the olfactory epithelium of the roof and the upper surfaces of the conchae; (4) the drainage — the openings of the paranasal sinuses (frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, sphenoid) empty into the meatuses; (5) the mucosal lining — ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium that warms, humidifies and filters the inspired air. It persists as a standard anatomical region in otolaryngology, rhinology and endoscopic sinus surgery references. e.g.: the nasal cavity in the sagittal section of Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; the inferior nasal concha visualized on anterior rhinoscopy in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the olfactory cleft mapped during endoscopic sinus surgery | not: the nasopharynx (the region below the nasal cavity opening into the oropharynx); the paranasal sinus (the bony cavity beside the nasal cavity that opens into it) [formal: cavum nasale | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The pulmonary artery is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the arterial conduits carrying deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle of the heart to the pulmonary capillary beds for gas exchange. Parameters: (1) the truncus pulmonalis (pulmonary trunk) — the main outflow tract arising from the right ventricle, approximately 5 cm in length; (2) the right and left pulmonary arteries — the trunk bifurcates at the sternocostal surface of the pericardium, with the right artery crossing anterior to the ascending aorta and esophagus to reach the right lung, and the left artery arching over the left main bronchus to reach the left lung; (3) the arterial wall — composed of tunica intima, tunica media rich in elastic lamina (proportionally more elastic than systemic arteries at equivalent diameter), and tunica adventitia, reflecting the low-pressure, high-compliance nature of the pulmonary circulation; (4) the bronchial anastomoses — distal connections with bronchial arteries (systemic circulation) providing collateral supply to the lung parenchyma. It persists as a defined anatomical region in cardiology, pulmonology, and thoracic surgery. e.g.: the pulmonary trunk as visualized on cardiac MRI at the American Journal of Roology; the right pulmonary artery's course anterior to the ascending aorta described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; CT pulmonary angiography showing left pulmonary artery embolism per European Radiology guidelines | not: the pulmonary vein (returns oxygenated blood to left atrium, not an artery); the systemic pulmonary collateral artery (a pathological accessory vessel, not the canonical pulmonary arteries) [formal: arteria pulmonalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The pulmonary vein is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the four venous conduits that carry oxygenated blood from the pulmonary capillary beds of both lungs to the left atrium of the heart. Parameters: (1) the right and left superior pulmonary veins — draining the upper lobes of each lung; (2) the right and left inferior pulmonary veins — draining the lower lobes and lingula, running obliquely through the lung parenchyma before piercing the fibrous pericardium; (3) the venous wall — composed of three tunics (intima, media, adventitia) but with a thinner media than corresponding pulmonary arteries, lacking the prominent elastic lamina of their arterial counterparts; (4) the ostial region — the proximal segments within the left atrial wall where ectopic pacemaker foci originate in atrial fibrillation, clinically targeted during pulmonary vein isolation ablation. It persists as a defined anatomical landmark in cardiology, pulmonology, and electrophysiology. e.g.: four pulmonary veins on transesophageal echocardiography per ASE guidelines; CT pulmonary venous anatomy prior to left atrial appendage occlusion per JCE; pulmonary vein stenosis following radiofrequency ablation in European Heart Journal | not: the pulmonary artery (carries deoxygenated blood from heart to lungs, not a vein); pulmonary collateral vein (pathological connection, not one of the four canonical pulmonary veins) [formal: vena pulmonalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: bronchiole
payload.scope: People made the bronchiole construct to map the small cartilage-free conducting airways that convey air from the bronchial tree to the respiratory zone, so that pulmonologists can localize small-airway disease and interpret bronchial conductive resistance.

definition.body: The bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the branching system of small conducting airways, each under 1 mm internal diameter with no cartilage in its wall, extending from the terminal bronchus to the respiratory zone. Parameters: (1) the origin, arising where the bronchial cartilage plates disappear (about the 11th to 13th generation from the trachea) and branching to the respiratory zone; (2) the wall structure, lacking cartilage and goblet cells, with a thin tunica propria of smooth muscle and elastic tissue so that lumen caliber is set by smooth-muscle tone and airway resistance rather than by cartilage; (3) the conducting function, in which the progressively increasing total cross-sectional area makes the bronchiole the dominant site of bronchial conductive resistance, with the mucociliary escalator continuing to the terminal bronchiole; (4) the boundary, the membranous bronchiole being the most distal purely conducting airway, beyond which the respiratory bronchiole opens directly into the alveolar ducts and alveoli, a transitional rather than purely conducting structure; (5) the clinical relevance, airway obstruction and mucus retention occurring in the cartilage-free bronchiole (small-airway disease), imaged by high-resolution CT mosaic attenuation from air trapping. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in pulmonology, respiratory physiology, and histology. e.g.: the bronchiole as described in West's Respiratory Physiology, 10th edition; high-resolution CT mosaic attenuation from air trapping distal to an obstructed bronchiole; FEV1/FVC ratio in small-airway obstruction per ATS/ERS spirometry standardization | not: the respiratory bronchiole (the transitional airway opening directly into alveoli); the alveolus (the gas-exchange sac distal to the bronchiole); the bronchus (the cartilage-bearing airway proximal to the bronchiole) [formal: bronchiolus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pulmonary-hilum
payload.scope: People made the pulmonary-hilum construct to map the medial entry-and-exit zone of each lung where its bronchus, vessels, and nerves enter and exit, so that radiologists can stage hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and thoracic surgeons can plan hilar dissection.

definition.body: The pulmonary hilum is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the oval zone on the mediastinal (medial) surface of each lung where the bronchus, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, and pulmonary nerves enter and exit. Parameters: (1) the contents — the main bronchus, the superior and inferior pulmonary veins, the lobar pulmonary artery, the bronchial vessels, the hilar lymph nodes (IASLC station 10, the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary node groups), and the vagal and phrenic nerve branches; (2) the arrangement — on the right the pulmonary artery lies anterior to the bronchus with the inferior pulmonary vein lowest, while on the left the arching pulmonary artery is most superior, the bronchus posterior, and the veins inferior; (3) the boundary — the hilum is a named zone on the mediastinal surface of the lung rather than a structural partition, delimited by the fissures and the pulmonary ligament, and its contents are identified by their relations; (4) the clinical role — the site of the hilar lymph node stations (IASLC stations 10 and 11), the target of CT and PET staging, and the operative plane of hilar dissection and pneumonectomy in lung-cancer surgery. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in thoracic radiology, thoracic surgery, and pulmonology. e.g.: the pulmonary hilum as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; CT chest showing right hilar lymphadenopathy in a patient with small-cell lung cancer; hilar lymph node dissection during lung-cancer surgery per NCCN guidelines | not: the mediastinum (the central thoracic compartment, a larger zone holding the hilar contents); the carina (the ridge at the tracheal bifurcation, superior and medial to the hilum); the bronchus (the conducting airway passing through the hilum, a named structure, not the zone) [formal: hilum pulmonis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: respiratory-bronchiole
payload.scope: People made the respiratory bronchiole construct to map the transitional airway between conducting bronchioles and alveolar ducts, where sparse alveoli appear in its wall and limited gas exchange begins, so that pathologists can identify the respiratory zone and clinicians can localize the site of early smoke-induced parenchymal damage.

definition.body: The respiratory bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the transitional conducting-to-gas-exchange airway branching from the terminal bronchiole. Parameters: (1) the origin, arising as a direct branch of the terminal bronchiole at about the 17th to 19th generation from the trachea; (2) the wall structure, lacking cartilage and submucosal glands, with a thin wall interrupted by scattered alveolar outpouchings so that it is neither purely conducting nor purely alveolar; (3) the epithelial transition, lined by simple cuboidal Clara cells and ciliated cells proximally, becoming increasingly alveolar distally as the wall is progressively replaced by gas-exchange openings; (4) the smooth-muscle component, a thin circumferential layer surrounding the origin of each alveolar sac, providing some control over airflow into the respiratory zone; (5) the functional gradient, in which the proportion of gas-exchange surface increases distally so that the most distal respiratory bronchioles consist almost entirely of alveoli with only a short blind-ending conducting lumen. It persists as a maintained landmark in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, and occupational lung pathology. e.g.: the respiratory bronchiole as described in Junqueira Basic Histology, 15th edition; terminal respiratory unit architecture in West Respiratory Physiology, 10th edition; centriacinar emphysema centered on respiratory bronchioles per GOLD criteria for COPD | not: the terminal bronchiole (the most distal purely conducting airway without alveolar outpouchings); the alveolus (the dedicated gas-exchange sac without any conducting lumen); the bronchiole (the cartilage-free conducting airway proximal to the transitional zone) [formal: bronchiolus respiratorius | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lobar-bronchus
payload.scope: People made the lobar bronchus construct to map each named airway branch that enters a specific lung lobe through the pulmonary hilum, so that thoracic surgeons can isolate individual lobes during lobectomy and radiologists can localize lobar consolidations.

definition.body: The lobar bronchus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps each major branch of the main bronchus that supplies a single pulmonary lobe. Parameters: (1) the division, arising from the main bronchus where it bifurcates into lobar branches — three on the right (superior, middle, and inferior lobar bronchi) and two on the left (superior and inferior lobar bronchi); (2) the cartilaginous support, containing hyaline cartilage plates in the wall at the point of divergence from the main bronchus, decreasing in number toward the periphery of the lobar branch; (3) the segmental supply, each lobar bronchus further dividing into segmental bronchi that supply individual bronchopulmonary segments — the right upper lobe bronchus gives rise to apical, anterior, and posterior segmental bronchi; the left upper lobe bronchus supplies the lingular and non-lingular segments; (4) the access route, each lobar bronchus is directly reachable by flexible bronchoscopy through the main bronchus and is the target of lobar-bronchus isolation in bronchoscopic lung volume reduction procedures. It persists as a maintained landmark in thoracic surgery, bronchoscopy, and pulmonology. e.g.: the lobar bronchus as described in Gray s Anatomy, 42nd edition; right middle lobe bronchus isolation during video-assisted thoracoscopic lobectomy; segmental bronchus targeting for endobronchial valve placement | not: the main bronchus (the larger airway proximal to the lobar branches, diverging from the carina); the segmental bronchus (the smaller subdivision within a lobe, branching from the lobar bronchus); the trachea (the airway above the main bronchi) [formal: bronchus lobaris | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: artery
payload.scope: People made the artery construct to map blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart, providing the high-pressure conduit system that delivers oxygenated blood to tissues or deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

definition.body: The artery is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps vessels transporting blood away from the heart under systemic or pulmonary pressure. Parameters: (1) the lumen — the internal diameter through which blood flows, maintained open by the vessel wall's structural integrity; (2) the wall architecture — three tunics (intima: endothelial lining and subendothelial connective tissue; media: smooth muscle and elastic fibers providing contractile and distensible properties; adventitia: collagenous connective tissue anchoring the vessel to surrounding structures); (3) the elastic-artery / muscular-artery distinction — elastic arteries contain abundant elastic lamellae in the media for Windkessel function, while muscular arteries have a thicker muscular media with fewer elastic elements; (4) the branching hierarchy — arteries progressively bifurcate and reduce in diameter from the great vessels (aorta, pulmonary trunk) through elastic arteries, muscular arteries, to arterioles. It persists as a maintained structural classification in anatomy, physiology, cardiology, and vascular surgery. e.g.: the aorta as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; coronary artery bypass grafting procedure; the internal elastic lamina of the human femoral artery in histological cross-section | not: the capillary (the microscopic exchange vessel with a wall consisting of a single endothelial cell layer); the vein (carries blood toward the heart, lower pressure, thinner walls) [formal: arteria | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vein
payload.scope: People made the vein construct to map blood vessels that carry blood toward the heart, providing the low-pressure return conduit that collects deoxygenated blood from tissues or oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the heart.

definition.body: The vein is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps vessels transporting blood toward the heart under low pressure. Parameters: (1) the lumen — the internal diameter through which blood flows, often larger than a companion artery's with thinner walls; (2) the wall architecture — three tunics (intima: endothelial lining; media: thin layer of smooth muscle and few elastic fibers; adventitia: collagenous connective tissue), with media proportionally thinner than the corresponding artery; (3) the valve system — intraluminal folds of the intima reinforced with connective tissue that prevent retrograde flow, particularly abundant in the extremities where hydrostatic pressure opposes venous return; (4) the capacitance function — veins accommodate ~60–70% of total blood volume at rest, acting as a blood reservoir whose tone is modulated by sympathetic nervous activity. It persists as a maintained structural classification in anatomy, physiology, cardiology, and vascular surgery. e.g.: the superior vena cava as described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; saphenous vein harvest for coronary artery bypass grafting; central venous catheter placement in the internal jugular vein | not: the capillary (the microscopic exchange vessel with a wall consisting of a single endothelial cell layer); the arteriole (the small terminal arterial branch regulating flow into capillary beds) [formal: venae | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pulmonary-artery
payload.scope: People made the pulmonary-artery construct to map the vessels that carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for gas exchange, so that radiologists can evaluate pulmonary embolism and surgeons can access the pulmonary vasculature.

definition.body: The pulmonary artery is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the vessels carrying deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle of the heart to the capillary networks of both lungs. Parameters: (1) the main pulmonary trunk — arising from the right ventricle, ascending anteriorly and to the left, then bifurcating at the level of the sternal angle (T6) into right and left pulmonary arteries; (2) the right pulmonary artery — the longer vessel passing horizontally behind the ascending aorta and superior vena cava to enter the right lung hilum; (3) the left pulmonary artery — the shorter vessel arching over the left main bronchus and anterior to the descending aorta to enter the left lung hilum; (4) the wall architecture — three tunics (intima, media, adventitia) with elastic fibers in the media providing distensibility to accommodate right ventricular stroke volume; (5) the segmental division — each main pulmonary artery divides to accompany the corresponding bronchus into lobar and segmental branches. It persists as a maintained landmark in radiology, cardiothoracic surgery, and pulmonology. e.g.: the pulmonary trunk as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; CT pulmonary angiography for diagnosis of pulmonary embolism; right pulmonary artery sling congenital anomaly in pediatric radiology | not: the pulmonary vein (returns oxygenated blood to the left atrium, not from the heart); the bronchial artery (carries oxygenated blood from the aorta to lung tissue, a systemic vessel) [formal: arteria pulmonalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: bronchiole
payload.scope: People made the bronchiole construct to map the small-caliber cartilage-free airways branching from the main bronchi down to the terminal bronchioles, so that clinicians can understand the conducting zone of the lung, diagnose obstructive airway diseases, and interpret the site of aerosol drug deposition.

definition.body: The bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the small-caliber airways branching from the main bronchi and terminating at the terminal bronchioles. Parameters: (1) the caliber threshold — airways less than 1 mm in internal diameter, distinguished from bronchi by the absence of cartilage plates in the wall; (2) the wall architecture — a mucosa lined by simple cuboidal epithelium (ciliated cells and Clara cells), a submucosa without glands, a layer of smooth muscle bundles arranged spirally around the lumen, and an outer connective tissue layer; (3) the cartilage boundary — the transition from bronchus to bronchiole marked by the abrupt disappearance of hyaline cartilage plates from the airway wall; (4) the muscular control — the circumferential smooth muscle layer regulated by autonomic innervation (vagal parasympathetic causing constriction, sympathetic causing dilation) allowing regulation of airflow resistance; (5) the generation range — extending approximately from the 4th to the 16th respiratory generation, branching dichotomously to produce thousands of terminal bronchioles. It persists as a maintained landmark in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, and obstructive lung disease. e.g.: the bronchiole as described in Junqueira Basic Histology, 15th edition; pulmonary function testing showing airflow obstruction at the small-airway level per ATS guidelines; histology slide of human bronchiole wall showing cuboidal epithelium and smooth muscle layer stained with H&E | not: the bronchus; the terminal bronchiole; the respiratory-bronchiole [formal: bronchiolus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: alveolar-duct
payload.scope: People made the alveolar-duct construct to map the thin-walled gas-exchanging airways that follow the respiratory bronchioles and open into the alveolar sacs, so that histologists and physiologists can trace the transition from the conducting airway to the gas-exchange unit within the pulmonary acinus.

definition.body: The alveolar duct is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the thin-walled gas-exchanging airway distal to the respiratory bronchiole and proximal to the alveolar sac, whose wall is studded with alveoli. Parameters: (1) position in the acinus — the segment of the respiratory airway tree following the respiratory bronchiole and leading into the alveolar sac, so the conducting path runs terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct, alveolar sac, alveolus; (2) the wall architecture — a smooth-muscle layer without cartilage, its wall perforated by the mouths of the alveoli that line it; (3) the epithelial lining — simple cuboidal to squamous epithelium of alveolar type I and type II pneumocytes continuous with the neighbouring alveoli; (4) the ductal neck — the short transitional segment joining the alveolar duct to the alveolar sac. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, and radiology. e.g.: the alveolar duct as described in Junqueira Basic Histology, 15th edition; a lung histology section showing alveolar ducts ringed by alveoli on H&E; the alveolar duct segment in the acinus diagram of West's Respiratory Physiology, 10th edition | not: the respiratory bronchiole (the transitional airway with scattered alveoli on a bronchiolar wall); the alveolar sac (the terminal cluster of alveoli sharing a common opening); the terminal bronchiole (the last purely conducting airway, without gas exchange) [formal: ductus alveolaris | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: bronchopulmonary-segment
payload.scope: People made the bronchopulmonary-segment construct to map each discrete anatomic unit of a lobe that carries its own segmental bronchus and bronchial arterial branch, so that surgeons can plan segmentectomy and radiologists can localize disease to a named segment.

definition.body: The bronchopulmonary segment is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps each discrete anatomic unit of a pulmonary lobe served by one segmental bronchus and its accompanying bronchial arterial branch. Parameters: (1) the definition of the unit — a segment is the portion of lung parenchyma drained and supplied by a single named segmental bronchus, so the segment is the anatomic correlate of the named segmental airways of the accepted bronchus construct (10 named segments in the right lung, 8-10 in the left); (2) the vascular signature — each segment carries its own branch of the bronchial artery, so the parenchyma can be devascularized and resected without destroying neighboring segments; (3) the intersegmental plane — each segment is separated from its neighbors by intersegmental veins that drain through the connective tissue between segments rather than through the segment's own parenchyma; (4) the clinical unit — the segment is the standard unit of anatomic segmentectomy and of radiologic localization of focal disease, with the right upper lobe divided into apical, posterior, and anterior segments and the right lower lobe into superior, medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, and posterior basal segments. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in thoracic surgery, thoracic radiology, and pulmonary histology. e.g.: apical segmentectomy of the right upper lobe performed for a stage IA non-small cell lung cancer per NCCN guidelines; the superior segment of the left lower lobe identified on HRCT for localization of a solitary pulmonary nodule; the right middle lobe lateral segment described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition | not: the pulmonary lobe (the larger division that contains several segments, divided by fissures); the segmental bronchus (the airway serving a segment, part of the accepted bronchus construct, not the parenchymal unit); the alveolus (the microscopic gas-exchange sac, the segment's terminal tissue, not the unit itself) [formal: lobulus pulmonis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lobe
payload.scope: People made the lobe construct to map each named division of a lung cut off by its interlobar fissures, so that surgeons can plan lobectomy and radiologists can localize disease to a named lobe.

definition.body: The lobe is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps each named division of a lung set off by its interlobar fissures. Parameters: (1) the division — the right lung carries three lobes (upper, middle, and lower) separated by the horizontal and oblique fissures, and the left lung carries two lobes (upper and lower) separated by the oblique fissure, the left upper lobe bearing the lingula in place of a middle lobe; (2) the airway signature — each lobe is entered by its own lobar bronchus, the named branch of the main bronchus (three right, two left), so the lobe is the anatomic unit served by a lobar airway; (3) the segmental organization — each lobe is subdivided into bronchopulmonary segments served by segmental bronchi, so the lobe is the intermediate level of the bronchial tree's accepted hierarchy (main, lobar, segmental, subsegmental); (4) the clinical unit — the lobe is the standard unit of anatomic lobectomy and of radiologic reporting, where consolidation is described by lobe (for example, right lower lobe consolidation). It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in thoracic surgery, thoracic radiology, and pulmonology. e.g.: right lower lobectomy performed for a stage II non-small cell lung cancer per NCCN guidelines; left upper lobe consolidation on chest CT in lobar pneumonia; the lingula described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition | not: the bronchopulmonary-segment (the smaller division within a lobe, separated by intersegmental planes, not fissures); the lung (the whole organ containing the lobes); the mediastinum (the central compartment between the two lungs, not a division of either) [formal: lobus pulmonis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: segmental-bronchus
payload.scope: People made the segmental-bronchus construct to map each named airway branch arising from a lobar bronchus and supplying a single bronchopulmonary segment, so that thoracic surgeons can perform segmentectomy and bronchoscopists can localize disease to a specific lobar region.

definition.body: The segmental bronchus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps each named airway branch arising from a lobar bronchus that supplies a single bronchopulmonary segment, representing the third-order branching of the bronchial tree. Parameters: (1) the hierarchy — on the right, the right upper lobar bronchus divides into apical, anterior, and posterior segmental bronchi (3 segments); the right middle lobar bronchus gives rise to the medial and lateral segmental bronchi (2 segments); the right lower lobar bronchus gives rise to the superior segmental bronchus and 3-4 basal segmental bronchi (4-5 segments), totaling 10 segmental bronchi on the right. On the left, the left upper lobar bronchus divides into the anterior segmental bronchus supplying the lingula and the posterior-superior segmental bronchus dividing into apical-posterior and inferior segmental bronchi, while the left lower lobar bronchus supplies 4-5 segmental bronchi, totaling 8-10 segmental bronchi on the left; (2) the cartilaginous wall — irregular plates of hyaline cartilage maintain patency, with cartilage amount intermediate between lobar and subsegmental bronchi; (3) the segmental correspondence — each segmental bronchus corresponds to one bronchopulmonary segment, its parenchymal territory drained by the accompanying branch of the bronchial artery and bordered by intersegmental veins; (4) the bronchoscopic target — each segmental bronchus ostium is visible by rigid or flexible bronchoscopy and serves as a landmark for segment-specific interventions including endobronchial valve placement, balloon occlusion, and targeted biopsy. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in pulmonology, thoracic surgery, and bronchoscopic practice. | not: the lobar bronchus (the second-order branch supplying a lobe, proximal to segmental divisions); the subsegmental bronchus (the smaller branch distal to segmental bronchi, not yet accepted as an entry); the bronchopulmonary segment (the parenchymal unit served by the segmental bronchus, a distinct concept) e.g.: Right upper lobe apical segmental bronchus (B1); Left lower lobe superior segmental bronchus (B6); Gray's Anatomy 42nd edition right middle lobe lateral segmental bronchus (B5) | not: Lobar bronchus (proximal second-order branch); Subsegmental bronchus (distal to segmental); Bronchopulmonary segment (parenchymal unit) [formal: bronchus segmentalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: terminal-bronchiole
payload.scope: People made the terminal-bronchiole construct to map the last purely conducting airway before the respiratory zone begins, so that pathologists can identify the conducting-respiratory transition and clinicians can localize small-airways disease.

definition.body: The terminal bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the last purely conducting segment of the bronchial tree, branching from the subsegmental bronchus and giving rise to respiratory bronchioles, with no gas-exchange function in its wall. Parameters: (1) the positional hierarchy — branching from the subsegmental (metabronchiolar) airway at approximately the 16th to 19th generation from the trachea, each terminal bronchiole serves as the final conducting conduit for its respiratory unit; (2) the wall architecture — lined by simple cuboidal epithelium, primarily Club cells (Clara cells) and ciliated cells, lacking cartilage plates and submucosal glands; (3) the smooth-muscle sleeve — a circumferential ring of smooth muscle at the distal tip, providing the primary mechanism for bronchoconstriction at the terminal conducting level; (4) the Club cell population — prominent non-ciliated Club cells that secrete club cell secretory protein (CCSP/CC10), metabolize xenobiotics via cytochrome P450 enzymes, and serve as progenitor cells for the bronchiolar epithelium. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in pulmonary histology, respiratory physiology, and occupational lung pathology. | not: the subsegmental bronchus (the conducting airway proximal to terminal bronchiole, still contains cartilage); the respiratory bronchiole (the transitional airway where gas exchange begins); the bronchiole (the general class of cartilage-free conducting airways, proximal to the terminal level) e.g.: Terminal bronchiole histology described in Junqueira Basic Histology 15th edition; terminal bronchiole Club cell pathology in West Respiratory Physiology 10th edition; small airways disease assessment by terminal bronchiole narrowing in GOLD criteria for COPD | not: Subsegmental bronchus (proximal conducting airway); Respiratory bronchiole (transitional with alveoli); General bronchiole (proximal to terminal level) [formal: bronchiolus terminalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: subsegmental-bronchus
payload.scope: People made the subsegmental-bronchus construct to map the airway level between the segmental bronchi and the cartilage-free bronchioles, so that bronchoscopists can navigate the last cartilage-bearing generation and histologists can mark the bronchial-bronchiolar transition.

definition.body: The subsegmental bronchus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the airway branches between the segmental bronchi and the bronchioles, the last airway generation still bearing hyaline cartilage plates.
